documents.unit: Office of the Provost (University Academic Regulations)
documents.title: Code of Academic Integrity (University Academic Regulations, Bulletin 2026-2027)
documents.stance_why: The code's AI clause says misuse of AI 'to circumvent learning goals' is a violation, lists 'accessing or using AI tools without authorization' and failure to acknowledge AI contributions, and says 'What constitutes use or misuse of AI will differ depending on context and discipline.' AI use is unauthorized unless permitted, but permission is left to a 'Course AI Policy', so the document restricts by default while leaving specifics to courses; it is the only AI text and offers no tiers. Restrict fits better than delegates because unauthorized use is declared misuse.
documents.summary: The University of Portland's academic integrity code adds 'Misuse of AI' as a fourth violation category beside cheating, forgery and plagiarism, naming undisclosed AI-generated work, unauthorized AI use and unacknowledged AI contributions. The rest is the general penalty levels and reporting, review and appeal process, which now applies to AI cases; the faculty member must supply the written 'Course AI Policy' when reporting an AI violation.

units.why: The code puts AI misuse in the same class as cheating or plagiarism: 'considered a violation of academic integrity comparable to cheating or plagiarism'. That is the definition of P36 (misconduct classification); it is a statement of fact, so modality informs.
units.anchor: considered a violation of academic integrity comparable to cheating or plagiarism
units.frag_start: The misuse of artificial intelligence

units.why: This sentence defines what the AI clause covers: misuse 'to circumvent learning goals or to engage in research misconduct'. It sets scope rather than a rule, so P61; the research-misconduct half is part of the same definition, not a separate P62 rule.
units.anchor: misuse of artificial intelligence technologies (AI) to circumvent learning goals
units.frag_start: The misuse of artificial intelligence
units.fit_note: Also names research misconduct as a covered kind of misuse, which P61 does not capture.

units.why: It says 'What constitutes use or misuse of AI will differ depending on context and discipline', so the line is not fixed centrally. P04 (setting varies by instructor/assignment) is nearest; P109 (aligning with discipline norms) does not fit since nobody is told to coordinate.
units.anchor: What constitutes use or misuse of AI will differ depending on context and discipline.
units.frag_start: What constitutes use or misuse
units.fit_note: Says context and discipline decide, not specifically the instructor or assignment.

units.why: The first listed example of misuse is 'submitting work generated by AI as one's own without proper acknowledgement'. That is a ban on passing off AI-generated work (P19), here conditioned on lack of acknowledgement; P24 covers the acknowledgement duty separately.
units.anchor: submitting work generated by AI as one’s own without proper acknowledgement
units.frag_start: submitting work generated by AI
units.fit_note: The ban applies to work submitted without acknowledgement; the text does not say acknowledged AI work is allowed.

units.why: The second example, 'accessing or using AI tools without authorization', makes AI use misuse unless authorized. That is an authorization-required rule (P107) rather than a tier or a syllabus-silence rule.
units.anchor: accessing or using AI tools without authorization
units.frag_start: accessing or using AI tools
units.fit_note: Does not say who authorizes (the 'Course AI Policy' later suggests the instructor).

units.why: The third example, 'failure to acknowledge AI-generated contributions to an assignment or other academic work', requires students to acknowledge AI contributions, so P24 (disclose with each submission). Failing to disclose is itself named a violation, which also touches P28.
units.anchor: failure to acknowledge AI-generated contributions to an assignment or other academic work
units.frag_start: failure to acknowledge AI-generated
units.fit_note: Nondisclosure is named as a violation (P28 aspect) but no format is given.

units.why: The code tells students to 'consult directly with their teachers' for more precise information; AI is among the examples. Closest is P10 (ask before using), though the sentence is about all violations, not AI use specifically.
units.anchor: Students should consult directly with their teachers.
units.frag_start: Students should consult directly with
units.fit_note: Applies to all integrity violations, not only AI, and is about asking for precise information, not about uncertain uses.

units.why: It says 'Ignorance of these or other breaches of academic integrity will not be deemed ... an excuse', so students must learn the rules (P78) or be held responsible. It covers AI because the AI clause is among the examples. P78 fits only partly, since it is generic.
units.anchor: Ignorance of these or other breaches of academic integrity will not be deemed
units.frag_start: Ignorance of these or other
units.fit_note: Generic across all integrity violations; stated as a no-excuse rule rather than a duty to read course rules.

units.why: The code says all violations 'will be penalized as appropriate' with consideration of 'a first offense or a repeat offense', which is penalty scaling by offense history. P37 states penalties in advance (escalation by offense); it fits partly since actual penalties are set later by level.
units.anchor: whether or not this is a first offense or a repeat offense
units.frag_start: All violations of academic integrity will
units.fit_note: Lists factors (knowledge, intention, nature, first or repeat) for choosing the penalty, not a fixed penalty.

units.why: The sentence assigns penalty decisions: 'at the discretion of the provost and dean or their designees'. It names who decides penalties, so P80 (who owns/enforces), not P37 since it gives no penalty itself.
units.anchor: at the discretion of the provost and dean or their designees

units.why: Level 1 penalties are described as 'educative rather than punitive', so a first, unintentional violation is handled as a learning matter. P68 (respond educatively) fits better than P37 because the point is the educative stance.
units.anchor: Penalties are educative rather than punitive
units.frag_start: Penalties are educative rather than
units.fit_note: Covers Level 1 penalties only; Levels 2 to 4 are not educative in this wording.

units.why: Level 1 conditions: 'lack of knowledge' and 'not intentional and ... first offense', which treats good-faith first offenses as lower level. It defines the level rather than the response, so P37 (penalty escalation by offense) is chosen over P68.
units.anchor: The violation is not intentional and is the first offense.
units.frag_start: Level 1 violations may occur because
units.fit_note: Defines the level criteria rather than stating a penalty.

units.why: Level 1 lists concrete penalties such as 'requiring the student to rewrite a paper for a minimally passing grade', which is a stated penalty in advance (P37).
units.anchor: requiring the student to rewrite a paper for a minimally passing grade
units.frag_start: Penalties are educative rather than punitive
units.frag_end: community service for a specified number of hours.
units.policy: Level 1 penalties may include making up the assignment, rewriting a paper for a minimally passing grade, acquiring specific knowledge related to ethics, and community service for a specified number of hours.

units.why: Level 2 penalties include 'assigning a failing grade in the course', a concrete sanction listed in advance for more serious, partly intentional violations (P37).
units.anchor: assigning a failing grade in the course
units.frag_start: Penalties may include: [1] an academic warning
units.frag_end: what was learned from the experience.
units.policy: Level 2 penalties may include an academic warning of up to one year, no credit for the work, a failing grade in the course, and a short paper on the ethical issues of the violation.

units.why: Level 3 penalties include 'suspension from the University for one or more semesters', listed in advance for intentional, premeditated violations (P37).
units.anchor: suspension from the University for one or more semesters
units.frag_start: academic probation for a stated period
units.policy: Level 3 penalties may include academic probation, a failing grade in the course, restitution for damages, suspension from the University for one or more semesters, and withdrawal of University funding.

units.why: Level 4 penalties include 'revocation of an awarded degree' and 'dismissal from the University', the most severe stated sanctions (P37).
units.anchor: revocation of an awarded degree
units.frag_start: Penalties may include: [1] dismissal from the University
units.policy: Level 4 penalties may include dismissal from the University, permanent notation on the student's transcript, restitution for damages, and revocation of an awarded degree.

units.why: The code lets repeated or severe violations end in 'temporary suspension or permanent dismissal', an escalation by offense that applies to AI misuse as an integrity violation (P37).

units.why: When a violation is likely, 'the faculty member must report the violation to his or her associate dean' with a memorandum and recommended penalty, a required reporting step (P81).

units.why: The university frames integrity as a community responsibility: each person is 'responsible for encouraging academic integrity in others ... and for reporting breaches to the appropriate authorities'. It applies to AI misuse as an integrity breach; P81 (reporting) is closest, and the duty is general.
units.anchor: for reporting breaches to the appropriate authorities
units.frag_start: each person is responsible for encouraging
units.fit_note: A general duty on everyone to encourage integrity, confront and report breaches, not AI-specific.

units.why: The code grounds its standard in being 'a scholarly community in the Roman Catholic tradition' that promotes 'respect, honesty, and fairness'. That is a values-based reason for integrity, not skill-building, so P95.
units.anchor: promotes respect, honesty, and fairness in service to God and neighbor
units.frag_start: The University’s interest in maintaining compliance
units.fit_note: The reason is religious and moral identity, a wider basis than fairness to other students.

units.why: Each person is 'accountable to the University not only for their own individual actions ... but also for the actions of groups of which they are a part', so members own what they and their groups produce (P29), including group work with AI.
units.anchor: accountable to the University not only for their own individual actions
units.frag_start: each person who participates in the mission
units.frag_end: groups of which they are a part.
units.fit_note: Extends accountability to groups a person belongs to; not specific to AI.

notes: Only one included document; the code is general, so only the Misuse of AI clause is AI-specific. Process and penalty units are coded because they govern AI cases (the code refers to a 'Course AI Policy' in the reporting step). Several procedural units use P81 with fit notes.
